Harness (src/harness/pico3/harness.ts) — pico3 task-kind scheduler with conversations, hooks, tasks, and config; opened with Harness.open.
createAgentHarness (src/harness/runtime/harness.ts) — Factory that restores session state and builds the harness runtime.
MemoryStorage (src/harness/session/memory.ts) — In-memory Storage implementation; also MemoryStorageOptions class with fork.
JsonlStorage (src/harness/session/jsonl/storage.ts) — JSONL-based Storage with v4 format and v3 legacy migration/upgrade.
MemorySessionRepo (src/harness/session/memory.ts) — In-memory session repository implementing SessionRepo.
JsonlSessionRepo (src/harness/session/jsonl/repo.ts) — JSONL session repository with create/open/list/delete/fork and legacy v3 support.
sessionRepoBenchmarkTargets (benchmark/session/session-repo-targets.ts) — Benchmark fixture for memory session repo.
storageBenchmarkTargets (benchmark/session/storage-targets.ts) — Benchmark fixture for memory storage.
registerReadBenchmarks (benchmark/session/benchmark.ts) — Registers read benchmarks; also registerWriteBenchmarks.
apply (docs/mobile-handoff/01-harness/01-delta/delta.ts) — Applies a list of Op deltas to a target object.
createBashTool (src/harness/tools/bash.ts) — Bash tool with timeout validation and output capture; also createReadTool/createEditTool/createWriteTool.
HarnessEventBus (src/harness/events.ts) — Event bus for harness events with watch support and resnapshot.
createGate (src/harness/execution/effect-gate.ts) — Gate for admitting tool/effect execution with abort signal.
loadSkills (src/harness/skills.ts) — Load skills from directories with frontmatter and ignore patterns; also loadPromptTemplates.
generateBranchSummary (src/harness/compaction/branch-summarization.ts) — Generate branch summary after navigation using LLM; also collectEntriesForBranchSummary.
compact (src/harness/compaction/compaction.ts) — Generate compaction summary with retries; also prepareCompaction, shouldCompact, estimateTokens.

chunks.heading: Packages Ai
chunks.text: This module contains the AI streaming runtime for the pi repository: provider adapters for a dozen AI APIs (Anthropic Messages, OpenAI Completions/Responses/Codex, Google Generative AI/Vertex, Bedrock, Mistral, etc.), the models registry, auth flows (API key and OAuth device/browser flows), message type definitions, and a large scripted model data generation toolchain. The core is the `Models` class tying providers, credentials, model catalogs, and streaming together, with per-provider `stream`/`streamSimple` adapters that translate the unified transcript/event model to each wire protocol. Also includes utilities for SSE parsing, JSON repair, retries, context overflow detection, and token estimation.

chunks.heading: Packages Ai — key points
chunks.text:
Unified streaming interface: every provider (e.g., anthropic-messages, openai-completions, bedrock-converse-stream) exports a `stream` and `streamSimple` function returning an `AssistantMessageEventStream` that emits a normalized event sequence, while provider-specific options types (AnthropicOptions, BedrockOptions, etc.) extend StreamOptions in src/api/types and in each adapter's file.
The `Models` class (src/models.ts) is the public façade: it registers providers, refreshes model catalogs with network fetches and manifest-based validation (scripts/model-data.ts), resolves auth credentials, and applies per-request transforms such as header injection and prompt-cache session keys.
Auth is split into API-key resolution (src/auth/resolve.ts, src/env-api-keys.ts) and OAuth flows per provider (src/auth/oauth/*, e.g., anthropic.ts, github-copilot.ts, openai-codex.ts); OAuth flows support local callback servers, device code polling, token refresh, and lazy module loading through src/auth/oauth/load.ts.
Model data is generated by scripts/generate-models.ts and generate-image-models.ts, which fetch provider catalogs (OpenRouter, Together, NVIDIA, etc.) at build time; src/scripts/model-data.ts validates the generated directory against a manifest with exact model-id assertions and a JSON structure hash.
Event processing utilities live in src/utils/: assistant-message-frame.ts converts raw provider events into a compact frame format (with tool-call catch-up), json-parse.ts repairs malformed streamed JSON, event-stream.ts implements the FIFO queue behind AssistantMessageEventStream, and overflow.ts/retry.ts classify error messages to detect context overflow, retryable failures, and rate limits.

chunks.heading: Packages Ai — entry points
chunks.text:
stream (packages/ai/src/api/anthropic-messages.ts) — Adapter for the Anthropic Messages SSE API: builds params, handles OAuth and header merging, decodes SSE events into text/thinking/toolcall deltas, and computes usage. Also manages beta features like fine-grained tool streaming.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/openai-completions.ts) — Adapter for OpenAI-compatible chat completions (used by openrouter, together, etc.). Handles reasoning fields (reasoning_content, reasoning_details), tool call streaming with grammar-constrained input properties, and provider compat flags like cache control format.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/bedrock-converse-stream.ts) — Adapter for AWS Bedrock ConverseStream using the SDK client. Resolves region/credentials from ARN, env, or explicit options, supports bearer-token auth, custom headers via middleware, and stream events for text/thinking/tool calls with redacted reasoning.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/openai-responses.ts) — Adapter for the OpenAI Responses API, on top of the shared processResponsesStream in openai-responses-shared.ts. Handles reasoning items, tool calls, and service-tier based pricing.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/openai-codex-responses.ts) — Adapter for OpenAI Codex with a WebSocket-first transport that falls back to SSE. Compresses request bodies with zstd, manages websocket session cache/fallback, and handles rate-limit retry logic.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/bedrock-converse-stream.ts) — Adapter for AWS Bedrock ConverseStream using the SDK client. Resolves region/credentials from ARN, env, or explicit options, supports bearer-token auth, custom headers via middleware, and stream events for text/thinking/tool calls with redacted reasoning.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/openai-responses.ts) — Adapter for the OpenAI Responses API, on top of the shared processResponsesStream in openai-responses-shared.ts. Handles reasoning items, tool calls, and service-tier based pricing.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/openai-codex-responses.ts) — Adapter for OpenAI Codex with a WebSocket-first transport that falls back to SSE. Compresses request bodies with zstd, manages websocket session cache/fallback, and handles rate-limit retry logic.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/mistral-conversations.ts) — Adapter for Mistral's chat API, supporting SSE streaming, tool calls, prompt caching, and reasoning effort/prompt-mode options.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/google-generative-ai.ts) — Adapter for Google's Generative AI (Gemini) SDK, streaming content parts into thinking/text blocks with thought signatures, and reasoning levels or token budgets.
stream (packages/ai/src/api/google-vertex.ts) — Adapter for Google Vertex AI, sharing conversion helpers with google-generative-ai via google-shared.ts. Supports API-key or ADC-based auth and custom base URLs.
createModels (packages/ai/src/models.ts) — (via Models interface) Factory for a Models instance that wires up providers, credential store, auth context, and refresh generation tracking. But entry point not directly exported; see createModels in src/models.ts.
createImagesModels (packages/ai/src/images-models.ts) — Factory for the image-generation equivalent of Models, wrapping images providers (currently openrouter-images) with auth resolution and generateImages dispatch.
registerBuiltInApiProviders (packages/ai/src/compat.ts) — Registers the built-in API streaming adapters into the registry (with lazy loading wrappers). Also exports stream/complete/streamSimple/completeSimple functions for resolving a model's api to its adapter.
builtinProviders (packages/ai/src/providers/all.ts) — Constructs the list of built-in provider instances (each with auth config, model lists, and streaming entry points), used by compat and model store.
registerBundledOAuthFlowLoaders (packages/ai/src/auth/oauth/load.ts) — Allows bundlers to substitute OAuth module loaders (e.g., in Bun) so only the requested provider's OAuth code is pulled in at runtime.

chunks.heading: Packages Chord
chunks.text: Chord is the structural module for packages/chord, implementing a facet-based application architecture. It provides a delta-based state tracking system for JSON data, a dependency-injected service framework with local and remote instances, facet lifecycle management, bundling/loading of facet bundles for Node.js, and serialization/validation of service wire protocol messages. Includes an immutable delta application API, reactive subscriptions with context propagation for cancellation, and node-specific tooling to package facets into distributable bundles with integrity manifests.

chunks.heading: Packages Chord — key points
chunks.text:
Provides delta-based state tracking: `track` observes mutations on JSON objects via proxies and emits compact operation lists (replace/set/delete/append/transform/patch) for efficient replication; `apply` applies ops to a target, `applyImmutable` creates new instances, and string diffs use suffix detection with configurable overlap scanning.
Facet lifecycle: `createFacetHost` in api.ts manages facets through states (setting_up → prepared → active → disposing → dead), topological ordering of dependencies, staged service activation, reload support detecting shape/reference changes, and disposal of owned resources.
Remote services: `RemoteServiceProvider` (provider.ts) classifies implementations into methods and replicated state members, validates them against RemoteServiceContract for JSON-compatible types, and supports singleton and keyed service instances with generation-based addresses, replacement (replacing implementations), spawning (creating keyed instances), subscriptions for state updates, and withdrawal.
Service wire encoding: `encoder`/`decoder` in delta/index.ts convert internal Ops to compact WireOps omitting implied paths during subscriptions; service-wire.ts defines wire snapshot/update formats with control calls (catalogue/subscribe/unsubscribe) and strict parsing/validation for cross-process communication.
Node bundling: `bundleFacets` (node/bundle.ts) uses esbuild to compile facet sources into a chord.facet-bundle format (version 2) with manifest chord-facets.json; `createFacetBundleLoader` loads and executes such bundles, resolving external imports via resolver or node require, verifying integrity hashes, and materializing artifact files.
Context system: context/index.ts provides immutable ContextKey/Context with BackgroundContext and TODO, value scoping, abort signal propagation/cancellation, and `awaitWithContext` to track pending operations; built-in ABORT_SIGNAL_CONTEXT_KEY integrates with cancellation flows.

chunks.heading: Packages Chord — entry points
chunks.text:
track (src/delta/index.ts) — Creates a Tracker wrapping a JSON object; mutations made through the returned proxy are recorded as delta Ops accessible via flush/rebase/discard. Used as the core change-tracking mechanism for replicated state.
apply (src/delta/index.ts) — Applies an array of Ops to a target object, mutating it in place; supports all op types and validates path safety/index ranges.
applyImmutable (src/delta/index.ts) — Applies Ops without mutating the input; copies containers along changed paths and returns a new object structure (for immutable state management).
createFacetHost (src/api.ts) — Async factory creating a FacetHost that manages facet lifecycles, service provision, and reloading; the main entry point for running facets.
defineService (src/api.ts) — Defines a Service with an ID and optional local-only flag; used to declare service contracts consumed/provided across facets and remote hosts.
createRemoteServiceBinding (src/api.ts) — Creates a RemoteServiceBinding that connects to a remote service provider via a transport, enabling use/observe of remote services with hydration and rebind support.
bundleFacets (src/node/bundle.ts) — Node-specific bundling of facet sources into distributable bundle artifacts with manifest and integrity checks; primary tool for packaging facets for deployment.
createFacetBundleLoader (src/node/bundle-loader.ts) — Creates a FacetLoader that loads a bundled facet artifact from disk, verifying manifest integrity and executing the bundle to extract facet definitions.
RemoteServiceProvider (src/services/provider.ts) — Central class for providing remote services; provide/withdraw/replace/spawn manage service implementations, and invoke/subscribe handle calls and state updates for bound clients.
createLoopbackServiceTransport (src/services/loopback.ts) — Creates a RemoteServiceTransport that routes calls/subscriptions directly to a given RemoteServiceProvider within the same process, used for testing and local facades.

chunks.heading: Packages Client
chunks.text: The packages/client module implements the client side of a remote service protocol. It provides a Client class for establishing connections, sending RPC requests, and subscribing to services, built on a byte-level transport abstraction. It includes Unix socket discovery and connection utilities, error handling, and promise helpers, with tests using an in-memory server for verification.

chunks.heading: Packages Client — key points
chunks.text:
Client class manages connection lifecycle (disconnected/connecting/connected), supports connect, reconnect, disconnect, and exposes state, server ID, and attachment info.
RPC via request(target, call, signal) returns ServiceResult (JsonValue | undefined); serviceCatalogue and subscribeService provide service discovery and subscription.
Connection class handles handshake, frame sending, and state changes; uses MAX_UINT32 for frame size limits and supports maxFrameLength.
Unix transport includes discoverUnixServers with timeout and concurrent probe limits, createUnixTransportFactory for socket connections, and handles socket lifecycle.
Errors: ServerError, DisconnectedError, ClientDisposedError; toError and toDisconnectedError convert unknown errors. PromiseResolvers helper for manual promise control.

chunks.heading: Packages Client — entry points
chunks.text:
Client (packages/client/src/client.ts) — Main client class: connect, request, subscribeService, dispose.
Connection (packages/client/src/connection.ts) — Manages connection state and frame transport.
discoverUnixServers (packages/client/src/unix.ts) — Discovers Unix socket servers with timeout and concurrency limits.
createUnixTransportFactory (packages/client/src/unix.ts) — Creates a ByteTransportFactory for Unix socket connections.
ServerError (packages/client/src/errors.ts) — Error class for protocol errors with code.

chunks.heading: Packages Coding Agent
chunks.text: The coding-agent package is the core implementation of the Pi coding agent. It provides the agent session runtime, manages model providers and authentication, implements built-in coding tools (bash, edit, read, write, grep, find, ls), handles session persistence, context compaction, and rendering. It includes a TUI-based interactive mode, print/JSON/RPC mode interfaces, and an experimental multi-process client/server architecture. A large set of example extensions demonstrates the extension API, ranging from custom tools and UI overlays to custom provider integrations.

chunks.heading: Packages Coding Agent — key points
chunks.text:
The package implements the Pi coding agent as a monolithic core with an `AgentSession` class orchestrating agent runs, message persistence, and extension event dispatch (src/core/agent-session.ts).
Built-in tools (bash, edit, write, read, grep, find, ls, powershell) are implemented as pluggable definitions with renderers, enabling extension overrides and custom operations (src/core/tools/).
Model runtime abstracts provider composition, OAuth/API-key auth, models.json parsing, and remote provider catalog refresh, supporting numerous providers (src/core/model-runtime.ts, model-config.ts, provider-composer.ts).
Interactive mode provides a full TUI (theme engine, keybindings, selectors, session tree, overlays) and is the primary user interface (src/modes/interactive/), with print/json/rpc modes as alternative frontends.
An experimental client/server and session-worker architecture enables remote/attached sessions and plugin facets, using a coordinator for peer routing (src/experimental/).
The extension system loads .ts/.js modules, caches them per cwd, maps `@earendil-works/pi-*` aliases to bundled modules, and exposes an `ExtensionAPI` with tools, commands, shortcuts, events, and UI context (src/core/extensions/).
Context management includes auto-compaction (token-based, summarization), branch summarization, and cache warming to optimize provider usage (src/core/compaction/, cache-warmer.ts).
Sessions are persisted as versioned JSONL files with a tree structure; the SessionManager handles migration, branching, and rebuilding context (src/core/session-manager.ts).
A package manager resolves, installs, and updates extension/skill/prompt/theme packages from npm or git, integrating with settings (src/core/package-manager.ts).
The package includes extensive example extensions (e.g., custom provider Anthropic/GitLab, plan-mode, subagent, doom overlay) and an SDK example set demonstrating programmatic use (examples/)

chunks.heading: Packages Coding Agent — entry points
chunks.text:
AgentSession (packages/coding-agent/src/core/agent-session.ts) — Central session orchestrator: manages agent lifecycle, tools, extensions, compaction, retry, and event emission.
main (packages/coding-agent/src/main.ts) — CLI entry point: parses args, resolves sessions, and runs the selected mode (interactive/print/json/rpc).
parseArgs (packages/coding-agent/src/cli/args.ts) — Parses command-line arguments into an Args structure with validation.
InteractiveMode (packages/coding-agent/src/modes/interactive/interactive-mode.ts) — The interactive TUI mode: renders transcript, editor, footer, and handles keybindings and session commands.
createAgentSession (packages/coding-agent/src/core/sdk.ts) — SDK entry point to create an agent session programmatically.
ModelRuntime (packages/coding-agent/src/core/model-runtime.ts) — Manages model providers, credentials, and model availability; core for streaming and authentication.
SessionManager (packages/coding-agent/src/core/session-manager.ts) — Handles session persistence, tree navigation, and context building from JSONL files.
DefaultPackageManager (packages/coding-agent/src/core/package-manager.ts) — Resolves and installs extension/skill/prompt/theme packages from npm/git sources.
createExtensionRuntime (packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/loader.ts) — Creates the extension runtime context used by loaded extensions.
loadExtensions (packages/coding-agent/src/core/extensions/loader.ts) — Loads extension modules from paths and initializes them.
createToolDefinition (packages/coding-agent/src/core/tools/index.ts) — Builds tool definitions for built-in tools (read, bash, edit, etc.).
buildSystemPrompt (packages/coding-agent/src/core/system-prompt.ts) — Constructs the system prompt from resources, skills, and tool guidelines.
runRpcMode (packages/coding-agent/src/modes/rpc/rpc-mode.ts) — Runs the RPC protocol mode for external client control.
runPrintMode (packages/coding-agent/src/modes/print-mode.ts) — Runs print mode for non-interactive output pipelines.
startServer (packages/coding-agent/src/experimental/server.ts) — Starts the experimental persistent server for remote/attached sessions.

chunks.heading: Packages Durable
chunks.text: Packages Durable is a structural module providing the durable storage layer for conversations, entries, tasks, inputs, and documents. It defines core TypeScript types for records, storage operations, and outcomes, plus an in-memory implementation of the Storage interface.

chunks.heading: Packages Durable — key points
chunks.text:
Defines an in-memory storage implementation (MemoryStorage) that simulates the Storage interface for durable data, including conversations, entries, tasks, inputs, and commit sequencing.
Central types describe a content-addressed model with immutable IDs (Id = number), commit sequences (Seq), and a root conversation constant (ROOT_CONVERSATION_ID = 1).
Task lifecycle states are explicitly modeled: pending, running, and terminal, with outcomes spanning completed, failed, aborted, orphaned, and faulted.
Input records track deduplication via requestId and transition through queued, placed, done, and unanswered statuses.
Data manipulated by MemoryStorage is deep-cloned to protect caller-provided objects from unintended mutation during reads.
Entries support head markers, edits (omit/replace) for context overrides, and optional model messages and JSON data.
Storage API includes cursor-based pagination, findLatestHeadMarker for active head resolution, and write commits that return a sequence number.
MemoryStorage maintains sorted ID lists for efficient binary-search-based insertion and removal, enabling low-overhead scanning and pagination.
The module is structured as a compact package with only a handful of source files, relying on external context types (like Context) for operation metadata.
Tests cover behavior of MemoryStorage operations and type-level guarantees, including the Storage interface contract.

chunks.heading: Packages Durable — entry points
chunks.text:
MemoryStorage (packages/durable/src/memory-storage.ts) — Class implementing the Storage interface in-memory; primary implementation of durable storage without a backing database.
Storage (packages/durable/src/types.ts) — Interface defining the durable storage contract for operations like commit, scan, and retrieval across conversations, entries, tasks, and inputs.
TaskRecord (packages/durable/src/types.ts) — Type for durable task records with kind, version, input, dependencies (after), background flag, abort handling, and state machine.
EntryRecord (packages/durable/src/types.ts) — Type for conversation entries carrying kind, optional model messages, data payload, head reference, and context edits.
Input (packages/durable/src/types.ts) — Type for host-provided inputs with requestId deduplication and status transitions through the durable pipeline.

chunks.heading: Packages Evals
chunks.text: The packages/evals module runs documentation-effectiveness evaluations for the Pi coding agent. It builds Docker images with and without Pi documentation, runs eval cases against the agent, inspects model/provider configurations, and produces paired comparison reports measuring pass rates and metrics. The code orchestrates Docker, vitest, and custom harnesses to verify provider integrations, TUI rendering, and documentation impact.

chunks.heading: Packages Evals — key points
chunks.text:
Evaluations run in Docker containers with two variants: 'without_docs' (control) and 'with_docs' (treatment), comparing documentation's effect on agent performance.
The CLI (src/cli.ts) discovers *.docs.eval.ts files, builds images, runs tasks in Docker, and writes a comparison report; it uses a protocol digest for reproducibility.
Harnesses in src/harness.ts create agent sessions, prompt the agent, and extract outputs; PiCodingAgentHarness wraps the coding agent, and PiDocumentationEvalHarness adds docs-specific configuration.
Eval cases include OpenAI-compatible and custom streaming provider integration tests, model configuration checks, TUI context footer rendering, and documentation audit tool verification.
The report module (src/report.ts) pairs control and treatment runs, computes lift flags (no-lift, negative-delta, saturation, flaky), and formats a human-readable comparison report with operational totals.
Docker entrypoint (docker/entrypoint.ts) handles sandbox permissions, discovers tests, runs vitest, and writes artifacts; install-runtime.mjs packages workspace dependencies into the runtime image.

chunks.heading: Packages Evals — entry points
chunks.text:
createPiDocumentationEvalHarness (packages/evals/src/harness.ts) — Primary harness for documentation evals; runs the agent with given tools/models and extracts arbitrary output via the 'output' callback.
createPiCodingAgentHarness (packages/evals/src/harness.ts) — General harness for coding agent evals; supports noTools, customTools, workspace files, and system prompt transformation.

chunks.heading: Packages Protocol
chunks.text:
The packages/protocol module defines the wire protocol between client and server: message schemas validated at runtime, CBOR serialization, and length-prefixed frame decoding/encoding. It provides typed message abstractions (ClientMessage, ServerMessage) built on CBOR with strict validation, plus streaming decoders for framing.

Key design: protocol.ts uses TypeBox schemas to define a strict, versioned message envelope (version 8). Messages are CBOR-encoded; framing.ts adds a 4-byte length prefix (big-endian uint32). codec.ts wraps framing and CBOR with validation/type-checking into a push-based decoder streaming interface. CBOR implementation is self-contained with safety limits (max depth 64, max byte length 16 MiB).

Packages exchange: client sends hello/request/cancel; server sends hello/hello_error/response/service_update/attachment. Validation errors are surfaced as ProtocolValidationError or FrameError during decode. Constants like PROTOCOL_VERSION and DEFAULT_MAX_FRAME_LENGTH live in protocol.ts and framing.ts respectively.

The structured entry points are encodeCbor/decodeCbor (cbor), encodeFrame/FrameDecoder (framing), encodeClientMessage/encodeServerMessage and ClientMessageDecoder/ServerMessageDecoder (codec), and parseClientMessage/parseServerMessage (codec) — the latter produce typed, validated objects from raw decoded values.

chunks.heading: Packages Protocol — key points
chunks.text:
Defines a versioned protocol (PROTOCOL_VERSION=8) with strict message schemas in protocol.ts using TypeBox, validated at runtime against a union of client/server message variants (ClientMessage, ServerMessage).
CBOR codec implements full RFC 8949 with safety limits: max depth 64, max byte/container length 16 MiB, configurable via CborOptions; encodeCbor/decodeCbor are the primary entry points.
Framing adds a 4-byte length prefix; FrameDecoder handles incremental push of chunks, produces complete frames, enforces max frame length via FrameDecoderOptions; encodeFrame produces the prefixed bytes.
codec.ts separates concerns: parseClientMessage/parseServerMessage validate raw decoded values; ClientMessageDecoder/ServerMessageDecoder combine framing+CBOR parsing into a streaming API with push/end, raising ProtocolValidationError or FrameError on malformed data.
Test coverage confirms wire compatibility; tests include CBOR known-vector hex strings (e.g., empty array '80', map with a:1,b:[2,3] 'a26161016162820203') and protocol hello messages.

chunks.heading: Packages Server
chunks.text: This package implements a server for a remote procedure call (RPC) protocol. It manages client connections over a byte-oriented transport, processes incoming messages, and routes service calls to hosted sessions. The server tracks sessions, handles client attachment/detachment, and coordinates lifecycle events such as handshaking, closing, and error handling. It includes a Unix socket listener for transport and a testing harness for protocol verification.

chunks.heading: Packages Server — key points
chunks.text:
The server orchestrates connections via a `Server` class that accepts `ByteConnection`s, handles the handshake protocol, and dispatches messages to session/service logic.
Session routing is handled by `SessionRouter`, which manages hosted sessions, client attachments, and serializes operations per client to maintain consistency.
Errors are categorized using a `ServerError` hierarchy with specific codes like `SessionNotFoundError` and `ServerDrainingError` to signal protocol-appropriate failures.
The Unix listener (`UnixListener`) provides a socket-based transport with socket file management, stale socket cleanup, and configurable modes/timeouts.
A comprehensive testing layer (`TestHarness`, `ProtocolTestClient`) allows simulating client behavior and service responses to validate the server's protocol implementation.

chunks.heading: Packages Server — entry points
chunks.text:

SessionRouter (packages/server/src/session-router.ts) — Manages session lifecycle including attach/detach, service call execution, and session removal. Used internally by `Server`.
createTestServer (packages/server/src/testing/server.ts) — Testing utility to create a configured test server, useful for integration and protocol tests.
ProtocolTestClient (packages/server/src/testing/client.ts) — Simulates a protocol client for testing, capable of sending raw bytes/fragmented messages and asserting server responses.

chunks.heading: Packages Session Backends
chunks.text: This module provides SQLite-backed session persistence for the agent runtime. It implements the session repository and storage abstractions using SQLite as the storage engine, supporting sessions, branches, values, entries, and usage tracking. The sqlite-node package contains the Node.js-specific SQLite adapter, SQL query helpers, repository implementation, and comprehensive tests including conformance and benchmark suites. Sessions are stored as individual SQLite database files (or shared database containers), with a schema covering sessions, entries, branch memberships, scalar/list values, and usage ledgers. The repository manages session lifecycle (create/open/list/delete/fork), and storage handles mutations, queries, and snapshots for forking. The module includes conformance tests to ensure behavior matches the session/storage abstractions, plus benchmarks for performance validation.

chunks.heading: Packages Session Backends — key points
chunks.text:
SQLite-backed session persistence: each session stored as a separate .sqlite file (or shared database), with tables for sessions, entries, branch memberships, values (scalar/list), usage ledger, and sequence tracking.
Node.js adapter (createNodeSqliteFactory) wraps better-sqlite3 DatabaseSync into a SqliteDatabase interface supporting prepare/get/all/iterate, transactions, and open modes (create, existing, read-only).
SqliteSessionRepo implements the session lifecycle: create, open, list, delete, fork (with snapshot-based forking, copying entries/values to a new session), and close management with pending IDs and open storage tracking.
SqliteStorage implements the Storage interface: commit (transactional writes), getValue/scanValues/readList (typed value access), scanBranch (branch-aware entry queries with segment/compaction handling), snapshots for forking, and stats tracking.
Conformance and benchmark suites validate correctness against the session/storage contracts and performance targets, with dedicated benchmark scripts (session-repo.bench.ts, storage.bench.ts) exercising realistic workloads.

chunks.text:

SqliteOpenSession (packages/session-backends/sqlite-node/src/sqlite/session.ts) — Session facade wrapping storage and delegating operations (mutations, reads, branches, labels) with concurrency admission control.

chunks.heading: Packages Telemetry
chunks.text: This package defines a telemetry abstraction centered on spans, and provides an in-memory implementation plus a conformance test suite. It ships type-level machinery to validate telemetry schemas so that span names and their attributes are checked at compile time. The API is intentionally minimal (startSpan, setAttributes, addEvent, setStatus) and framework-agnostic, so adapters (like OpenTelemetry) can implement the same interface and pass the same conformance tests.

chunks.heading: Packages Telemetry — key points
chunks.text:
Defines a minimal TelemetryContext/TelemetrySpan interface with startSpan, setAttributes, addEvent, setStatus — no concrete adapter in this package, only an in-memory one.
The type system enforces telemetry schemas: defineTelemetrySchema() lets you describe spans, their start/end attributes, and events; derived types (TelemetrySchemaSpanStartAttributes, etc.) infer required vs optional attributes and reject unknown ones via ExactTelemetryAttributes.
createTypedSpanStarter() returns a typed starter that enforces the schema at compile time: the span name, its attributes, and the event names/attributes must match the declared schema, and it rejects duplicate span names across schemas.
InMemoryTelemetryContext records spans and events (with copied attribute values) so that tests can inspect them after execution; it also implements failure status propagation.
The package includes a conformance test generator (createTelemetryAdapterConformance) that any adapter can run to verify it behaves like the in-memory implementation — including error propagation and attribute handling.
NOOP_TELEMETRY_CONTEXT provides a no-op implementation for use when telemetry is disabled.

chunks.heading: Packages Telemetry — entry points
chunks.text:

chunks.heading: Packages Tui
chunks.text: The @earendil-works/pi-tui package is a terminal user interface library for Node.js. It provides a component model (Container, Text, Box, VStack/HStack, ScrollView), an editor with line editing, autocomplete, and undo, a full-screen alt-screen view with layout, mouse handling, selection, and search, terminal capability detection and image rendering (Kitty/iTerm2), keyboard input parsing (including Kitty and legacy sequences), LaTeX-to-Unicode rendering, and native platform helpers for clipboard and modifier keys on macOS, Linux, and Windows. It also defines a configurable keybinding system and a layout engine for full-screen mode. Native code for Linux and macOS lives in subdirectories with build scripts, while Windows builds are orchestrated by a Node script supporting MSVC or MinGW toolchains.

chunks.heading: Packages Tui — key points
chunks.text:
Component tree with layout: Container, Text, Box, HStack, VStack, ScrollView, Spacer, Loader, Image, Markdown, Input, Editor, SelectList, SettingsList, and overlay support via TUI.showOverlay; rendering is width-driven returning string[] lines.
Editor (src/components/editor.ts) is a full multiline editor with grapheme/word segmentation, kill-ring, undo stack, history, paste markers, autocomplete provider interface, and word-wrap; Input (src/components/input.ts) is a single-line version.
TuiAltScreen (src/tui-alt-screen.ts) provides fullscreen rendering with layout frame, mouse events (selection, click, wheel, scrollbar drag), search (AltScreenSearchComponent), Kitty image caching, and flash messages; TuiMainScreen (src/tui-main-screen.ts) handles regular terminal mode with diff-based rendering and image cleanup.
Input handling: keys.ts parses Kitty protocol, modifyOtherKeys, and legacy escape sequences into KeyIds; stdin-buffer.ts assembles chunks and detects bracketed paste; terminal.ts negotiates Kitty keyboard protocol and supports ProcessTerminal; keybindings.ts defines default keybindings for editor, input, select, and alt-screen.
LaTeX support (src/latex.ts) converts LaTeX commands and environments to Unicode with layout markers for fractions, roots, matrices, and operators; Markdown component (src/components/markdown.ts) renders Markdown with custom theme and LaTeX extensions.
Image support: terminal-image.ts detects capabilities via environment variables, encodes Kitty and iTerm2 image sequences, parses PNG/JPEG/GIF/WebP dimensions, and provides fallback placeholders.
Native platform integration: native-platform.ts loads platform-specific clipboard/helper modules; native-module-path.ts resolves native binary candidates; build.mjs (win32) chooses MSVC or MinGW toolchains based on environment.
Utility functions in utils.ts handle ANSI-aware text wrapping, truncation, slicing by column, background application, visible width, and grapheme segmentation; separate modules cover word navigation, fuzzy matching, kill-ring, and undo stack.

chunks.heading: .pi — key points
chunks.text:
Session import/export logic parses GitHub gist URLs, issue URLs, and pi.dev session share URLs into refs; supports extracting session data from exported HTML and JSONL.
The kaioken extension registers pi commands and tools with spend-gating, web ports, and a symbol oracle for grounding responses against the repository.
TUI components include animated boot/poweroff sequences, a kaioken logo, headers, and status panels with motion timing constants for carets and sweeping rules.
Hooks detect destructive commands (e.g., rm -rf, git push --force) and flag dirty state, with environment-controlled motion/color settings.

chunks.heading: Scripts
chunks.text: This is the scripts module of a monorepo. It contains 46 files, mostly JavaScript (mjs) and TypeScript scripts, plus a few shell scripts. The scripts cover a wide range of repository operations: smoke tests for agents, release and publishing workflows, generation of install locks and shrinkwraps, analysis of session and cost data, validation checks for entry graphs and package dependencies, and utilities for syncing versions. The module is structural, meaning these scripts orchestrate or analyze other parts of the repository rather than forming a cohesive library. Most code is procedural, often run via CLI, with a few test files for verification.

chunks.heading: Scripts — key points
chunks.text:
The module contains 46 files, mostly JavaScript (mjs) and TypeScript scripts, plus a few shell scripts, covering smoke tests, releases, dependency validation, and session analysis.
Several scripts handle release and publishing: `publish.mjs` checks and publishes workspace packages, `release.mjs` manages version bumps and changelogs, `publish-release-announcement.mjs` updates release pointers, and `local-release.mjs` builds package tarballs.
Dependency validation is a major theme: `check-pinned-deps.mjs` ensures exact versions, `check-runtime-deps.mjs` verifies runtime dependencies, `check-ts-relative-imports.mjs` enforces relative import rules, and `generate-coding-agent-install-lock.mjs` and `generate-coding-agent-shrinkwrap.mjs` create install locks to pin external dependencies.
Session analysis scripts (`edit-tool-stats.mjs`, `read-tool-stats.mjs`, `session-context-stats.mjs`, `tool-stats.ts`, `stats.ts`, `cost.ts`) parse JSONL session files from `~/.pi/agent/sessions` to produce reports on tool usage, token estimates, costs, and context window usage.
Some scripts are smoke tests (e.g., `agent-treeshake-smoke-entry.ts`, `browser-smoke-entry.ts`) that instantiate the Agent with a model and stream function, while others like `check-*` scripts validate internal consistency (e.g., entry graphs, kaioken barrels, offline compliance).

chunks.heading: const DESTRUCTIVE
chunks.text:
const DESTRUCTIVE = [ // Unix recursive force delete, in any flag spelling. /\brm\s+(?:-[a-z]*r[a-z]*\s+-[a-z]*f|-[a-z]*f[a-z]*\s+-[a-z]*r|--recursive[\s\S]*--force|--force[\s\S]*--recursive|-r[fF]|-f[rR])/i, // PowerShell recursive force delete, including the `ri`/`del` aliases. // No `\b` before the hyphenated flags: a word boundary needs a word/non-word // transition, and the space before `-Recurse` is not one, so `\b-recurse` // can never match. That single character is why `Remove-Item -Recurse // -Force` slipped through a guard that explicitly named powershell. /\b(?:remove-item|ri|del)\b[\s\S]*-recurse\b[\s\S]*-force\b/i, /\b(?:remove-item|ri|del)\b[\s\S]*-force\b[\s\S]*-recurse\b/i, // cmd.exe recursive quiet delete. /\bdel\s+[\s\S]*\/[sq]\b/i, // Disk-level destruction. /\b(?:format-volume|clear-disk|diskpart)\b/i, // History rewrites and discarding uncommitted work. /\bgit\s+push\b[\s\S]*--force(?!-with-lease)/i, /\bgit\s+reset\s+--hard\b/i, /\bgit\s+clean\b[\s\S]*\s-[a-z]*[fdx]/i, // Data loss. /\bdrop\s+(?:table|database|schema)\b/i, /\btruncate\s+table\b/i, ];
Commands that destroy work irreversibly.

This guard polices both `bash` and `powershell`, so it has to know both
vocabularies. It originally listed only Unix spellings (`rm -rf`, `drop
table`), which meant the destructive PowerShell idioms it claimed to cover
passed straight through — the hook named a shell it could not actually read.

The flag groups are written loosely because `rm -rf`, `rm -fr`, `rm -r -f`
and `rm --recursive --force` are the same command. Anything that only
rewrites a file in place is deliberately absent: over-blocking trains people
to route around the guard, which is worse than the gap.

chunks.heading: function applyKaiokenTheme
chunks.text:
function applyKaiokenTheme(ctx: ExtensionContext): void
Switch the session to the Kaioken theme, so the palette reaches every part of
the TUI rather than only the header.

The header's own colours come from the theme it is handed, so a theme that is
*installed but not selected* leaves the whole session — chat, tool output,
diffs, footer — on the built-in `dark` palette while the banner sits in
Kaioken orange above it. Applying it here is what makes the two agree.

Two deliberate limits:

- **It only applies when the theme exists.** `getTheme` returns undefined
  when `.pi/themes/kaioken.json` is absent — a checkout that never ran the
  build, or a user who deleted it. Falling back to a hard-coded palette would
  ignore their own choice, so nothing happens instead.
- **It is an instance, not a name.** `setTheme(name)` also writes the name to
  settings, which would silently rewrite the user's `theme` preference as a
  side effect of loading an extension. `setTheme(Theme)` sets it for this
  session only and leaves their setting alone.

`KAIOKEN_THEME=0` opts out entirely, and a user who has explicitly picked a
different theme is left where they are — the extension should not overrule a
deliberate choice, only fill in a default.

interface FakePi
A stand-in for Pi's `ExtensionAPI` so the bridge can be exercised without a
live session (Invariant 10: every test runs offline, with no keys).

The five bridge suites each grew their own copy of this, and they drifted:
some kept tools in an array, some in a map. None could fire a hook, so the
hook bodies — the code that decides whether a destructive command is blocked

chunks.heading: const CURTAIN
chunks.text:
const CURTAIN = { open: 700, close: 500, /** ~22fps. Fast enough that the beam's edge reads as sliding, not stepping. */ frameMs: 45, } as const;
Durations.

Not from DESIGN.md §2.5 — the keyframe matrix has no curtain in it, and
these are longer than anything in it on purpose. The first pass in v2 sat in
the `rise-in` family at half a second and was over before it registered: a
boundary marker nobody sees is not marking a boundary.

The opening is paced by its text, because typing has a legible speed — under
about eight milliseconds a character it stops reading as typing and starts
reading as a paint. The closing has nothing to read, sits between the quit
keystroke and the shell prompt coming back, and is a collapse rather than an
arrival, so it takes about two thirds as long.

end, the last character of the last line is on screen for a single frame
before Pi paints over it, which is the same as not having written it.

chunks.text:
const POWEROFF = { /** The wordmark sits there, whole, before the power is cut. */ hold: 0.16, /** The picture has finished collapsing into the beam. */ collapsed: 0.58, /** The beam has finished shrinking to a point. */ narrowed: 0.9, } as const;
Where the closing's phases hand over, as fractions of its duration.

This is not the opening reversed, and deliberately so. An entrance that
builds and an exit that un-builds are the same idea twice; what actually
happens when a terminal goes away is that the picture collapses into a line
and the line collapses into a point. Everyone who has switched off a CRT
knows this animation without being told what it is, which is exactly what
you want from the last half-second of a session.

chunks.heading: function hookBlock
chunks.text:
function hookBlock(exe: readonly string[], repo: string): string
The script we own.

Git runs hooks through `sh` even on Windows, so paths are written with
forward slashes and single-quoted: `sh` does no escape processing inside
single quotes, which sidesteps every question about how a backslash in
`C:\Users\…` would survive.

The refresh runs detached so it never delays a commit, and its output is
appended to `.kaioken/hook.log`: the previous `>/dev/null 2>&1` swallowed
every failure (missing node on the sh PATH, Windows file locks), leaving
no trace of why the wiki stopped refreshing.

chunks.heading: interface ExportManifest
chunks.text:
interface ExportManifest
Handoff bundle: every tenant's knowledge in one directory.

The point of an export is that the receiving side needs nothing installed —
no kaioken, no node_modules, no credentials. Everything is plain files:
cards as the JSON they are stored as, wiki documents as the Markdown a
person reads, skills and the graph beside them.

Layout, all under one directory:

    cards/<module>.json    knowledge cards, verbatim
    wiki/<path>            generated chapters and sections, verbatim
    skills/<name>          handwritten procedures, verbatim
    graph.json             the derived graph
    knowledge.md           the human-readable summary
    manifest.json          what is in the bundle, and where it came from

chunks.heading: function buildGraph
chunks.text:
function buildGraph(input: GraphBuildInput): KnowledgeGraph
Derive the knowledge graph from artifacts that already exist.

Deliberately a pure function of its input: nothing is read from disk here,
because the caller's mix of tenants differs (a repository may have cards but
no wiki, or neither), and because a graph that could only be built where the
filesystem looks one way would be a graph that tests could not build at all.

The edge rules are conservative on purpose. `shared_source` connects two
documents that provably draw on the same file; `references` connects a
document to another whose *source* it names. Neither invents a semantic

chunks.heading: function computeStaleness
chunks.text:
function computeStaleness( documents: readonly Provenance[], scan: ScanResult, options?: StalenessOptions, ): StalenessReport
Compute freshness by comparing recorded source hashes against the scan.

Deliberately deterministic and offline. This is the half of phase 5 that must
never break: a fresh clone with no credentials still has to be able to say how
far the code has moved past its documentation, and a system that presented
decayed documentation as current would be worse than one with none.

Nothing is stored. The report is derived on demand from two artifacts that
already exist, so it cannot drift out of sync with either.

Whole-file comparison is the default. When a source carries a `rangeHash`
binding and `options.symbolHashes` is provided, that source is judged against
its range hash instead, so edits outside the bound symbol or line range do
not mark the document stale.

This is the inverse lookup that makes selective regeneration possible: rather
than regenerating everything because something moved, match the moved files
against what each document was actually written from.

When `options.changedSymbols` is provided, symbol-bound sources match by
binding key instead of file path, so a file edit outside the bound range
does not invalidate the document. Without it, every source matches by path.

cost the same as generating from scratch and lose the point of the exercise.

when provided; otherwise they fall back to whole-file comparison.

Not a safety blanket — a boundary decision. Anything the research pipeline
would treat as evidence must be a page a person could read in a browser and
check with their own eyes.
`::1` is deliberately not here. As a suffix it also matches the public

Validating at lookup time before fetch prevents DNS rebinding and internal IP access

a 0-second TTL.

Rules: - Cite sources only as [N] where N is the exact number shown before a source block. - Attribute quotations directly: write "..." function verifyCitations( body: string, sources: readonly ResearchSource[], excerpts: readonly SourceExcerpt[], ): ResearchVerification
Verify a document's citations against the evidence.

A citation grounds when: the number names a fetched source, and — when the
claim includes a quoted string — the quote appears in that source's
sanitised text. Quote matching is whitespace-insensitive, because the
sanitizer normalises whitespace and the model does not.

Documents are prompted to write: claim, because the page says "..." [2].
The quote is the prose inside quotation marks immediately before the
bracket. Only a bounded span is taken — a quote must be checkable, not a
second document.

function rrf
chunks.text:
function rrf(lists: readonly (readonly Ranked[])[], limit: number): Ranked[]
Fuse any number of ranked lists: score = Σ 1/(k + rank) over every list an id
appears in.

Fusion is over *ranks*, not scores, which is the point: BM25 scores and cosine
similarities are not on a comparable scale, and normalising them against each
other would invent a relationship that does not exist.

must keep working with no credentials at all.

is why they are indexed at all: a procedure nobody can find is a procedure
nobody follows. The frontmatter is stripped rather than parsed, because the
only field that matters here is the name, and the layer that actually
validates a skill lives above this one.

This tenant is why `kaioken search` is useful the day it ships, before any
model has been called: the signatures and doc comments of a repository are
genuine derived knowledge about it, and they are the only knowledge that
exists after phase 1.

chunks.heading: function outline
chunks.text:
function outline(source: string): Heading[]
The headings of a document, in order.

A generated chapter is long by construction — it is written to cover every
export in scope — so arriving at the top of one with no map is the single
worst moment in reading the wiki. The renderer already assigns each heading a
slug; this extracts the same slugs so the navigation and the anchors cannot
disagree.

chunks.heading: function highlight
chunks.text:
function highlight(text: string, terms: readonly string[]): string
Escape text and mark the query terms inside it.

A result list where the reader has to re-find their own words in every snippet
makes them read all of them. Marking happens after escaping, so the only
markup that can reach the page is the `<mark>` this function writes.

A term only marks where a word starts. Marking anywhere would cut identifiers
into pieces — `handleWikiSearch` for the query "wiki search" — and a name
broken into three highlighted fragments is harder to read than an unmarked
one. Terms with no Latin letters are matched anywhere instead, because a
script that does not separate words has no word start to anchor to.

chunks.text:
function stripTitle(source: string, title: string): string
Drop the document's own title line.

A generated chapter opens with `# Title`, and the page already shows that
title in its header next to the freshness badge and the path. Rendering both
puts the same words on screen twice and pushes the first real sentence below
the fold.

function graphPage(): string
The full-bleed force-directed graph view, ported from kaioken v1: a canvas
driven by the embedded engine (`graphEngineAsset.ts`), plus a small filter
strip. Clicking a doc node navigates to `/d/<path>`; file nodes are inert —
there is no editor to open into. This is the one page in the site that
carries a script, and the one relationship view rich enough to need one.

Every tenant the search index returns has to be openable. Linking a card or a

chunks.heading: function leadDoc
chunks.text:
function leadDoc(chapter: WikiChapter): WikiDoc | undefined
The chapter's own opening document, when it has one.

A chapter index is titled after its chapter, so listing it as a child of that
chapter prints the same words twice and invites the reader to wonder what the
difference is. There is none: the chapter heading is the link to it.

chunks.heading: function verificationBadge
chunks.text:
function verificationBadge(doc: WikiDoc): string
Whether the verifier's claim checks held up.

This is deliberately separate from the freshness badge beside it. Freshness
asks "do the sources still match?" and grounding asks "were the claims about
them true?" — a document can be perfectly fresh and still have asserted
something false, so collapsing them into one label would hide exactly the
failure the verifier exists to catch.

chunks.heading: function verificationPanel
chunks.text:
function verificationPanel(doc: WikiDoc): string
The verifier's findings, including the ones that failed.

A badge saying "3 ungrounded" tells a reader to be suspicious and nothing
more. Naming the claim and its line turns that into something actionable,
which is the whole reason defects are persisted rather than counted.

chunks.heading: interface VerificationRecord
chunks.text:
interface VerificationRecord
What each generated document's verifier concluded.

Provenance answers "what was this written from"; this answers "did the claims
hold up". They are recorded separately because they fail independently — a
document can cite exactly the right files and still assert something false
about them, and a badge that conflated the two would report the second as
fine. Without this on disk there is nothing for a reader to check: the
per-document `defects` were computed, printed, and then dropped.

Defects are stored, not just counted. A count tells a reader to be suspicious;
the claim and its line tell them where to look.

chunks.heading: const BRIEF_SYSTEM
chunks.text:
const BRIEF_SYSTEM = `You are the principal engineer on this codebase, writing the ONE authoritative brief that every chapter of its documentation will be written from. Other writers will each see only their own files plus this brief, so it must carry the shared truth they cannot derive alone. Produce a compact markdown document, no more than about 80 lines, with exactly these sections: ## What this system is Two or three sentences: what it does and for whom. Concrete, not marketing. ## Architecture The real top-level components and how they relate. Name actual packages, directories and types from the input. State the dependency direction between them. ## Key flows The two or three most important paths through the system (a request, a job, a build), each as a short ordered list naming the real functions or files involved. ## Glossary The canonical name for each domain concept, one per line as "**Term** — definition". Include any term the codebase uses inconsistently, and state which name is canonical. Every chapter will be required to use these exact terms. ## Conventions Patterns a newcomer must follow: error handling, configuration, naming, layering. Only ones actually visible in the code. Rules: - Ground everything in the provided structure and sources. Never invent a component. - Name only files and declarations present in the evidence, because every chapter written from this brief is checked against the repository. - Output ONLY the markdown brief.`;
One brief, shared by every chapter.

Each chapter's writer sees only its own files, so terminology and top-level
structure are exactly what it cannot derive alone. Generating the shared
truth once and injecting it everywhere is what stops twelve chapters from
inventing twelve names for the same component.

chunks.heading: type Op
chunks.text:
type Op = | readonly ["r", JsonValue] | readonly ["s", NonEmptyPath, JsonValue] | readonly ["d", NonEmptyPath] | readonly ["a", NonEmptyPath, string] | readonly ["t", NonEmptyPath, number] | readonly ["p", Path, number, number, JsonValue[]];
Tuples are the form — in memory, on the wire, on disk.

`r` is the ONLY op that replaces a whole value. `s`/`d`/`a`/`t` cannot target
the root: the type forbids it. `p` may, and only because a tracked value can
itself be an array — but a `p` that replaces its entire target is normalised to
`r`/`s` at record time, so a root `p` is always a partial modification.

`Op` knows nothing about the path dictionary. Interning, id references and
omitted paths live in `WireOp` and exist only between `encode` and `decode`.

chunks.heading: type WireOp
chunks.text:
type WireOp = | readonly ["r", JsonValue] | readonly ["s", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, JsonValue] | readonly ["s", JsonValue] | readonly ["d", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>] | readonly ["d"] | readonly ["a", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, string] | readonly ["a", string] | readonly ["t", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, number] | readonly ["t", number] | readonly ["p", PathRef, number, number, JsonValue[]] | readonly ["p", number, number, JsonValue[]] | readonly ["#", number, Path];
What crosses a boundary. Adds two compressions and nothing else:

  ["#", id, path]    defines an id, emitted on a path's SECOND use
  a numeric PathRef  references a previously defined id
  a shortened tuple  reuses the previous op's path; arity disambiguates

["r", value] carries no path, so it encodes to itself — which is why isBase
works unchanged on either vocabulary.

chunks.heading: function dropDead
chunks.text:
function dropDead(ops: Op[]): Op[]
Drop ops that a later op makes unreachable.

Ops apply in order, so an op is dead if a later one overwrites the whole
subtree it lives in. Only `s`, `d` and `r` do that — `a`, `t` and `p` modify
what is already there, so they never dominate.

O(n * d): walk backwards keeping a map of overwritten paths, and for each op
test its own prefixes against that map. `d` is the path depth, which is small
and bounded. The obvious formulation — compare each op against every
dominator — is O(n^2 * d) and degrades on exactly the wide-flush input this
pass exists to clean up. Measured: 12-14 microseconds per op, flat from 100 to
5000 ops, and 10001 redundant writes collapse to 2 emitted ops.

OBJECT KEY ORDER IS NOT PRESERVED. A producer that does
`set c; set a; delete c; set c` leaves `c` last, because deleting and
reinserting moves it. The replica receives only the surviving `set c`, applies
it to a base where `c` never existed, and `c` lands first. Values are
identical — verified over 1823 randomised sequences with zero value
mismatches — but the serialised forms can differ.

This is fine because nothing compares a replica against its producer: the
consumer holds the state and nobody diffs it back. The one visible case is a
consumer that iterates keys for display, where two views could order rows
differently. It requires a delete-and-recreate of the same key within one
flush. Do not hash or content-address a replicated value.

chunks.heading: function assertValidOp
chunks.text:
function assertValidOp(op: unknown): void
Verb, arity and payload shape for a **decoded** op: paths inline, no `#`, no
short forms. `apply` uses this.

Validating `Op` against the wire grammar would be laxer than the type: a
two-element `["s", value]` would pass, and `apply` would then read the value as
a path. Each vocabulary gets the validator that matches it.

chunks.heading: function assertIndexInRange
chunks.text:
function assertIndexInRange(parent: readonly unknown[], index: number): void
An index may address an existing element or append exactly one past the end.

This is not an arbitrary cap — it is what keeps the value a `JsonValue`. A
sparse array does not survive a JSON round trip: holes serialise to `null` and
return as real properties, so `arr[7] = x` on a length-3 array already produces
state a replica cannot match. Rejecting the write is more honest than silently
diverging.

It also removes the denial of service it would otherwise permit:
`["s", ["xs", 4294967290], 1]` allocates a 4.29-billion-entry array from one op.
Growth stays possible and stays proportional — the tracker already emits
`arr.length = n` as a splice of explicit nulls, whose op size grows with the
gap, so a large growth costs a large op rather than a small one.

chunks.heading: type Op
chunks.text:
type Op = | readonly ["r", JsonValue] | readonly ["s", NonEmptyPath, JsonValue] | readonly ["d", NonEmptyPath] | readonly ["a", NonEmptyPath, string] | readonly ["t", NonEmptyPath, number] | readonly ["p", Path, number, number, JsonValue[]];
Tuples are the form — in memory, on the wire, on disk. There is no keyed
variant and no codec between them.

`r` is the ONLY op that replaces a whole value. It is an op rather than a
frame kind for the same reason `a` and `t` exist: they are specialisations of
`s` that are smaller and state intent. It also makes base detection a token
comparison rather than a path inspection, which matters because recovery stops
at the last base batch — a correctness boundary.

Only `p` may target the root, and only because a tracked value can itself be
an array. A `p` covering its entire target is normalised at RECORD time to `r`
or `s`, so a root `p` is always a partial modification.

The two-element forms reuse the previous op's path; arity disambiguates.

chunks.heading: type WireOp
chunks.text:
type WireOp = | readonly ["r", JsonValue] | readonly ["s", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, JsonValue] | readonly ["s", JsonValue] | readonly ["d", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>] | readonly ["d"] | readonly ["a", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, string] | readonly ["a", string] | readonly ["t", PathRef<NonEmptyPath>, number] | readonly ["t", number] | readonly ["p", PathRef, number, number, JsonValue[]] | readonly ["p", number, number, JsonValue[]] | readonly ["#", number, Path];

chunks.heading: method Tracker.flush
chunks.text:
flush(): Op[]
Drain. Empty when nothing changed.

The FIRST flush is always a base batch, carrying the value including any
mutations made before it — a consumer starts with nothing, so a stream must
open with something to apply deltas to.

Ops that a later op makes unreachable are dropped first — a field written
three times emits one op, and a parent replaced after its child emits one.
Object key order is not preserved by that pass; see `delta.md` §5.

chunks.heading: class OutputCapture
chunks.text:
class OutputCapture
Bounded capture for a Shell implementation.

Owns the two-stage structure that `shell-output.ts` had inside `bash.ts`: a raw
buffer trimmed to `maxBytes * 2` as a memory guard, and a retained view
computed from it per snapshot. `truncateTail` is line-aware — it walks
backwards line by line and takes a partial only when one line alone exceeds the
cap — so eviction is not byte arithmetic and cannot be done incrementally.

Emits the three update kinds from `executionenv.md` §4 and enforces the
ordering invariant: once the cap is crossed, a `chunk` never follows without an
intervening `snapshot`.

chunks.heading: function createCompartment
chunks.text:
async function createCompartment({ memoryLimit = 256 } = {})
A membrane between the host realm and an isolated-vm isolate.

── The safety argument, which is structural, not a convention ──────────────

isolated-vm CAN be used unsafely. The documented footgun is handing the guest
a live handle to a host object — via `derefInto()`, or by returning a
`Reference` from a host call — after which the guest can walk that object's
prototype chain into the host realm.

This membrane makes that impossible by construction rather than by care:

  1. `encode()` is the ONLY way a host value reaches the guest, and it is
     `JSON.stringify` with a replacer. Its output is a string. A string
     cannot carry a reference.
  2. Host callables do not cross. They are replaced by an integer id into
     `hostTable`, which lives entirely host-side. The guest receives a number.
  3. Exactly ONE `Reference` is ever given to the guest — `__invokeRef`, the
     single call-in point — and its `deref()` throws cross-isolate ("Cannot
     dereference this from current isolate"). Its `derefInto()` yields an
     inert `Dereference` marker: not callable, no host globals.
  4. `derefInto()` is used exactly once, on the guest's OWN global. No host
     object is ever an argument to it.

The consequence: the guest's entire view of the host is `{ number, string }`.
There is no object graph to walk, so there is nothing to walk it into. This is
the same property the QuickJS membrane has, and it is why the choice between
them is about performance and packaging rather than about safety.

Verified by `src/escape-audit.ts`.

chunks.heading: function declareToolChanges
chunks.text:
function declareToolChanges(context: AgentContext, pendingMessages: AgentMessage[]): AgentMessage[]
Declare tool loadout changes to the model.

`context.tools` is what the runtime can execute; the transcript's system messages declare
what the model may call. Before each request the difference becomes `toolsAdded` and
`toolsRemoved` on a system message. When a pending system message exists, its tool fields
are treated as intent and replaced with the delta between the committed transcript and
the executable set, so replay always yields exactly `context.tools`. Otherwise a new
system message is inserted before the first non-system pending message.

chunks.heading: function failToolCallsFromTruncatedMessage
chunks.text:
async function failToolCallsFromTruncatedMessage( toolCalls: AgentToolCall[], emit: AgentEventSink, ): Promise<ExecutedToolCallBatch>
Fail all tool calls from an assistant message that was truncated by the
output token limit. Streamed tool-call arguments are finalized with a
best-effort JSON salvage parser, so a truncated message can yield tool calls
whose arguments parse and validate but are silently incomplete. None of them
are safe to execute; report each as an error so the model can re-issue them.

chunks.heading: method Agent.subscribe
chunks.text:
subscribe(listener: (event: AgentEvent, signal: AbortSignal) => Promise<void> | void): () => void
Subscribe to agent lifecycle events.

Listener promises are awaited in subscription order and are included in
the current run's settlement. Listeners also receive the active abort
signal for the current run.

`agent_end` is the final emitted event for a run, but the agent does not
become idle until all awaited listeners for that event have settled.

chunks.heading: class JsonlStorage
chunks.text:
class JsonlStorage extends MemoryStorage implements Storage
Files in a session directory:
  main.jsonl                   conversations, entries, inputs, rewindable/session doc ops, each task's
                               CREATE and TERMINAL records, and one marker per commit. Append-only, never rewritten.
  sticky-<conversation>.jsonl  sticky doc ops; rewritten from its last base by `truncate` (on the Session line)
  task-<id>.jsonl              a live task's intermediate patches (running, checkpoints); unlinked after its
                               terminal record is published in main

Publication (§10): one commit `Seq`; sidecar records are appended first, then exactly one main
record, last, listing the sidecar refs it expects — the publication point. Replay applies a sidecar
record only when main has the marker for that seq naming that file; unconfirmed sidecar tails are
ignored. Every record carries the committed-ID high-water. Bytes after the last newline of any file
are a torn write and are truncated before the file is opened for append. There is no compaction.

With `fsync: false`, recovery covers process termination while the OS and filesystem remain alive.
It does not promise that an acknowledged commit survives power loss, kernel/host failure,
storage-cache loss, or a filesystem that loses/reorders completed writes. An acknowledged tail may
roll back, or a surviving main marker may reference a missing sidecar and make open fail rather
than expose partial state. A lost pre-effect checkpoint can cause an external effect to be attempted
again; external idempotency remains required.

With `fsync: true`, each sidecar is flushed before the main publication marker is flushed. This
strengthens file-data durability and ordering across machine failure. It is not a complete database
guarantee: newly created files, renames, and unlinks are not followed by a parent-directory fsync,
and storage hardware/filesystems may provide weaker guarantees.

One process owns a directory at a time; a second process is unsupported.

chunks.heading: class Membrane
chunks.text:
class Membrane
A transaction-scoped revocable membrane over a Chord-tracked document.

Every object reached through a document proxy is wrapped lazily; all wrappers of one
transaction share one liveness flag; identity is preserved by a WeakMap. Mutations forward
to the underlying Chord proxy so its tracker records ops. At transaction finish — success,
callback failure, validation failure, storage failure — `revoke()` flips the flag and every
retained wrapper, root or nested, throws on any operation.

Assigning one wrapper into another (`a.list = b.list`) is rejected: Chord stores the value it
is given, and a stored proxy is the classic footgun. Assign plain values; splice in place.

chunks.heading: method Lane.readLane
chunks.text:
private async readLane<TResult>( read: (state: LaneState, reader: SessionReader) => TResult | Promise<TResult>, context: Context, ): Promise<TResult>
Run one effect-free command on this lane's serialized mutation line. Owned `state` is authoritative; the
planner receives that state plus a read-only reader for bounded payload lookups. Committed values and owned
state are immutable snapshots: update them by replacement, never in place. State-independent input validation
belongs before `command()`, while every state-dependent decision belongs inside its planner.

A planner may choose exactly one outcome:
- `commit` commits once, publishes `next`, then synchronously materializes the caller result from
  storage-assigned `CommitResult` metadata;
- `return` returns without a commit, boxed so a promise value is not awaited while holding the Session line;
- `reject` rejects outside the mutation/fault boundary as an expected caller error without a commit.

Planner, commit, and materialization errors fault the harness before releasing the Session line. Close/fault gates
are checked both before queueing and when the callback starts: close-first rejects, while a callback admitted
before close may finish its commit, publish memory, and resolve without another open check. Never invoke providers,
tools, hooks, timers, event handlers, or wait for task completion here; perform those after `command()` returns.

chunks.heading: function selectJsonlFork
chunks.text:
function selectJsonlFork(index: JsonlForkIndex, options: ForkOptions): ForkCurrentStatePlan
Validate the source lanes and return the fork plan.

Branch scope updates JsonlForkIndex's selected entries via index.selectEntry(): it selects the
destination tip and its ancestors after validating entryId and applying "at"/"before". The plan
records the branch name and destination tip; the copy pass uses the index to filter entries and labels.

Tree scope leaves the index's selected entries unchanged because the copy pass keeps every entry.
Both formats use the same indexed metadata; this function performs no file I/O.

chunks.heading: function indexForkInput
chunks.text:
async function indexForkInput( input: JsonlForkInput, fileSystem: FileSystem, context: Context, ): Promise<{ index: JsonlForkIndex; nextSeq: number }>
Build the index used to select branch ancestry and identify current scalar/list writes.
Retains entry parent links, current-row sequences, and lane inventory, not entry payloads.
Returns the index and the source's nextSeq high-water mark; no destination writes occur here.

V3: LegacyV3Source already scanned the file and assigned normalized IDs/sequences. Copy its
in-memory entry structures and derived values without reopening the file or calling writes(),
which would unnecessarily parse payloads and reconstruct compaction tails before fork selection.

V4: Open the source file and fold complete transactions into the index. For an open source,
stop at the captured commit-queue sequence boundary. For a closed source, scan to EOF or a torn
final line and derive nextSeq from the header and highest complete write sequence.
The later copy pass reopens the source file in both formats and emits only selected writes.

chunks.heading: function runJsonlFork

async function runJsonlFork( options: { input: JsonlForkInput; fileSystem: FileSystem; destinationPath: string; destinationHeader: Omit<JsonlStorageHeader, "nextSeq">; fork: ForkOptions; }, context: Context, ): Promise<void>
Index the source, validate the requested fork, and stream selected entries and current state
into an atomically published format-4 destination without modifying the source.
Preserve copied sequences and the source's nextSeq while excluding usage and open-operation state.
Source files must not be replaced or edited between passes; later append-only writes are excluded
by the captured sequence boundary or legacy record count. Does not open the destination Session.

async function loadSkills( env: ExecutionEnv, dirs: string | string[], context: Context, ): Promise<{ skills: Skill[]; diagnostics: SkillDiagnostic[] }>
Load skills from one or more directories.

Traverses directories recursively, loads `SKILL.md` files, loads direct root `.md` files with skill

function normalizeForFuzzyMatch(text: string): string
Normalize text for fuzzy matching. Applies progressive transformations:
- Strip trailing whitespace from each line
- Normalize smart quotes to ASCII equivalents
- Normalize Unicode dashes/hyphens to ASCII hyphen
- Normalize special Unicode spaces to regular space

chunks.heading: function applyReplacementsPreservingUnchangedLines
chunks.text:
function applyReplacementsPreservingUnchangedLines( originalContent: string, baseContent: string, replacements: TextReplacement[], ): string
Apply replacements matched against `baseContent` to `originalContent` while
preserving unchanged line blocks from the original.

This is useful when `baseContent` is a normalized view of the original. Each
replacement is widened to the lines it actually touches, those touched lines
are rewritten from the normalized base, and all other lines are copied back
from `originalContent`. The actual replacement ranges drive preservation so
duplicate normalized lines cannot be aligned to the wrong occurrence.

fuzzy-normalized version of the content (trailing whitespace stripped,
Unicode quotes/dashes normalized to ASCII).

chunks.heading: function applyEditsToNormalizedContent
chunks.text:
function applyEditsToNormalizedContent( normalizedContent: string, edits: Edit[], path: string, ): AppliedEditsResult
Apply one or more exact-text replacements to LF-normalized content.

All edits are matched against the same original content. Replacements are
then applied in reverse order so offsets remain stable. If any edit needs
fuzzy matching, the operation runs in fuzzy-normalized content space and then
overlays those line-level changes onto the original content so unchanged line
blocks keep their original bytes.

chunks.heading: class AdaptivePublisher
chunks.text:
class AdaptivePublisher<TValue, TUpdate>
Publishes the latest state without queuing intermediate mutations.

The first dirty state after idle is immediate. Each publication then buys a
delay proportional to its encoded size, with a minimum interval that also
bounds event count. A single trailing timer guarantees eventual publication.

chunks.heading: class OutputCapture

class OutputCapture
Maintains and publishes one bounded shell-output view.

Writes received while publication is rate-limited collapse into the latest
view. Small changes remain responsive; complete window turnovers purchase a
proportionally longer delay. The first update after idle and an explicit
final flush are immediate.

chunks.heading: type StreamFn
chunks.text:
type StreamFn = ( model: Model<Api>, context: TranscriptContext, options?: SimpleStreamOptions, ) => AssistantMessageEventStream | Promise<AssistantMessageEventStream>;
Stream function used by the agent loop. `Models.streamSimple` satisfies
this shape.

The loop passes a normalized transcript: the system prompt and tool
declarations are carried by the transcript's system messages, never by
`context.systemPrompt` or `context.tools`.

Contract:
- Must not throw or return a rejected promise for request/model/runtime failures.
- Must return an AssistantMessageEventStream.
- Failures must be encoded in the returned stream via protocol events and a
  final AssistantMessage with stopReason "error" or "aborted" and errorMessage.

chunks.heading: type ToolExecutionMode
chunks.text:
type ToolExecutionMode = "sequential" | "parallel";
Configuration for how tool calls from a single assistant message are executed.

- "sequential": each tool call is prepared, executed, and finalized before the next one starts.
- "parallel": tool calls are prepared sequentially, then allowed tools execute concurrently.
  `tool_execution_end` is emitted in tool completion order after each tool is finalized,
  while tool-result message artifacts are emitted later in assistant source order.

chunks.heading: type QueueMode
chunks.text:
type QueueMode = "all" | "one-at-a-time";
Controls how many queued user messages are injected when the agent loop reaches a queue drain point.

- "all": drain and inject every queued message at that point.
- "one-at-a-time": drain and inject only the oldest queued message, leaving the rest queued for later drain points.

chunks.heading: interface BeforeToolCallResult
chunks.text:
interface BeforeToolCallResult
Result returned from `beforeToolCall`.

Returning `{ block: true }` prevents the tool from executing. The loop emits an error tool result instead.
`reason` becomes the text shown in that error result. If omitted, a default blocked message is used.

chunks.heading: interface AfterToolCallResult
chunks.text:
interface AfterToolCallResult
Partial override returned from `afterToolCall`.

Merge semantics are field-by-field:
- `content`: if provided, replaces the tool result content array in full
- `details`: if provided, replaces the tool result details value in full
- `isError`: if provided, replaces the tool result error flag
- `usage`: if provided, replaces the tool result usage
- `terminate`: if provided, replaces the early-termination hint

Omitted fields keep the original executed tool result values.
There is no deep merge for `content`, `details`, or `usage`.
